title: Acid-Base Analyzer
sources: Brandis K. Acid-Base Physiology. changelog.change: Venous gas mode: a Sample toggle (arterial / venous). Venous values are converted to estimated arterial values with the Bloom 2014 pooled differences, then read with the same rules; flags mark the estimate, any read that leans on PCO2, and a normal venous PCO2 that makes hypercapnia unlikely (Cochrane 2025). Four venous golden vectors added (36 total).

Initial entry. One read-out from pH, PaCO2 and HCO3 (plus optional Na, Cl, albumin): pH status, primary disorder, expected compensation for all four primary disorders (acute and chronic for respiratory), second-disorder detection, albumin-corrected anion gap, delta ratio, hidden-acidosis check, and differentials. Engine parity-tested on web and iOS against 32 hand-worked golden vectors. Rules verified against Brandis §9.2, 9.3 and 3.3; citations verified on PubMed.

purpose: Reads a blood gas the way the stepwise method does: pH, primary disorder, expected compensation, a second disorder if compensation is off, then the anion gap and delta ratio. Enter pH, PCO₂ and HCO₃ from an arterial gas, or from a venous gas with the Venous toggle; add Na, Cl and albumin for the gap.

na.label: Na⁺
na.help: Optional — needed for the anion gap

cl.label: Cl⁻
cl.help: Optional — needed for the anion gap

albumin.label: Albumin
albumin.help: Optional — corrects the gap; low albumin hides a gap acidosis

sample.label: Sample
sample.help: Venous: arterial values are estimated (pH + 0.033, PCO₂ − 4.4, HCO₃⁻ − 1.0, pooled means). pH and HCO₃⁻ track arterial well; PCO₂ does not for an individual patient. Peripheral venous only — don't use for oxygenation.

chronicity.label: Respiratory process
chronicity.help: Only used when the primary disorder is respiratory. Renal compensation takes 2 to 3 days, so 'acute' and 'chronic' expect different HCO₃⁻ values.

phStatus.acidemia: Acidemia — an acidosis must be present
phStatus.alkalemia: Alkalemia — an alkalosis must be present
phStatus.normal: pH in range — either no disorder or an acidosis and an alkalosis offsetting each other

normal.label: No acid-base disorder on the gas
normal.detail: pH, PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ are all in range. Still check the anion gap: a gap acidosis and a metabolic alkalosis can cancel out.

metabolic_acidosis.label: Metabolic acidosis
metabolic_acidosis.detail: Low HCO₃⁻ drives the low pH. Check respiratory compensation with Winter's formula, then the anion gap.

metabolic_alkalosis.label: Metabolic alkalosis
metabolic_alkalosis.detail: High HCO₃⁻ drives the high pH. Gastric acid loss and diuretics cause about 90% of cases.

respiratory_acidosis.label: Respiratory acidosis
respiratory_acidosis.detail: High PaCO₂ drives the low pH. Nearly all cases are inadequate alveolar ventilation.

respiratory_alkalosis.label: Respiratory alkalosis
respiratory_alkalosis.detail: Low PaCO₂ drives the high pH. Hyperventilation is the mechanism in every case.

combined_acidosis.label: Combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis
combined_acidosis.detail: PaCO₂ is high and HCO₃⁻ is low: both processes push pH down, so a mixed disorder must be present. Typical of cardiac arrest or a tiring patient with a metabolic acidosis.

combined_alkalosis.label: Combined respiratory and metabolic alkalosis
combined_alkalosis.detail: PaCO₂ is low and HCO₃⁻ is high: both push pH up, so a mixed disorder must be present.

compensated_chronic_respiratory_acidosis.label: Compensated chronic respiratory acidosis
compensated_chronic_respiratory_acidosis.detail: PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ are both high with pH in range, and HCO₃⁻ matches the chronic 4-for-10 rule. A respiratory acidosis plus a metabolic alkalosis can look the same; the history decides.

compensated_chronic_respiratory_alkalosi.label: Compensated chronic respiratory alkalosis
compensated_chronic_respiratory_alkalosi.detail: PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ are both low with pH in range, and HCO₃⁻ matches the chronic 5-for-10 rule (the usual finding in pregnancy). A metabolic acidosis plus a respiratory alkalosis can look the same; the history decides.

respiratory_acidosis_with_metabolic_alka.label: Respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis
respiratory_acidosis_with_metabolic_alka.detail: Both PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ are high with pH in range, and HCO₃⁻ is above even the chronic expectation, so an extra metabolic alkalosis is present.

metabolic_acidosis_with_respiratory_alka.label: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis
metabolic_acidosis_with_respiratory_alka.detail: Both PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ are low with pH in range, and HCO₃⁻ is below the chronic respiratory expectation. Classic for salicylate toxicity, sepsis, and liver failure.

normal_ph_single_abnormal.label: pH in range with only one abnormal value
normal_ph_single_abnormal.detail: Only PaCO₂ or only HCO₃⁻ is outside its range. Recheck the entry or the sample before interpreting.

unclassified.label: Pattern not classifiable
unclassified.detail: The values do not fit a recognizable pattern. Recheck the entry or the sample.

compensation.appropriate: Compensation is as expected — no evidence of a second primary disorder.
compensation.plus_respiratory_acidosis: PaCO₂ is higher than expected — a respiratory acidosis is also present (fatigue, sedation, lung disease).
compensation.plus_respiratory_alkalosis: PaCO₂ is lower than expected — a respiratory alkalosis is also present.
compensation.plus_metabolic_alkalosis: HCO₃⁻ is higher than expected — a metabolic alkalosis is also present.
compensation.plus_metabolic_acidosis: HCO₃⁻ is lower than expected — a metabolic acidosis is also present.
compensation.fits_chronic: HCO₃⁻ fits a chronic (renally compensated) process.
compensation.acute_or_chronic: With this small PaCO₂ change, acute and chronic expectations overlap — the history decides.
compensation.between_acute_and_chronic: HCO₃⁻ sits between the acute and chronic expectations: acute-on-chronic, or renal compensation still developing. It can also be a mixed disorder; the history decides.

resp_acid.label: Respiratory acidosis
resp_acid.formula: HCO₃⁻ rises 1 (acute) or 4 (chronic) per 10 mmHg PaCO₂ above 40 (± 2)

resp_alk.label: Respiratory alkalosis
resp_alk.formula: HCO₃⁻ falls 2 (acute) or 5 (chronic) per 10 mmHg PaCO₂ below 40 (± 2)

anionGap.label: Anion gap
anionGap.correctedNote: Albumin-corrected: + 2.5 for each 1 g/dL albumin below 4.

deltaRatio.label: Delta ratio = (AG − 12) ÷ (24 − HCO₃⁻)
deltaRatio.caution: Built on four measured electrolytes and 'standard' normals — don't over-interpret; look for supporting evidence before acting on an unexpected value.

bands.hagma_plus_nagma: 0.4 to 0.8 — combined high-gap and normal-gap acidosis (note: often below 1 in renal failure).
bands.hagma: 0.8 to 2 — consistent with an uncomplicated high-gap acidosis (lactic acidosis averages about 1.6; DKA runs closer to 1).
bands.hagma_plus_high_hco3: Above 2 — HCO₃⁻ was high before the acidosis: a concurrent metabolic alkalosis, or a pre-existing compensated respiratory acidosis.

hh_inconsistent.text: pH, PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ don't agree with Henderson-Hasselbalch (more than 0.05 apart). Recheck the entry — a transcription error, or a serum total CO₂ entered in place of the gas HCO₃⁻.

albumin_not_entered.text: No albumin entered, so the gap is uncorrected. Low albumin lowers the gap and can hide a gap acidosis — common in critical illness.

hidden_acidosis_likely.text: Anion gap 20 to 30 without a metabolic acidosis on the gas — a gap acidosis is likely (about two-thirds of cases) and may be masked by a metabolic alkalosis.

hidden_acidosis_definite.text: Anion gap above 30 — a metabolic acidosis is present even though the gas doesn't show it. Look for an offsetting metabolic alkalosis.

enter_electrolytes_for_gap.text: Add Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (and albumin) to calculate the anion gap and delta ratio.

venous_estimate.text: Read from a venous gas: the analysis uses estimated arterial values (pH + 0.033, PCO₂ − 4.4 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ − 1.0 mmol/L, the pooled venous–arterial differences). The anion gap uses the measured HCO₃⁻, as serum chemistry would.

venous_pco2_unreliable.text: This read leans on PCO₂, which a venous gas can't pin down: individual venous–arterial differences run from about −20 to +26 mmHg. Treat the respiratory part (or the compensation check) as provisional, and get an arterial gas if it would change management.

venous_hypercapnia_unlikely.text: Venous PCO₂ is 45 mmHg or less, which makes arterial hypercapnia unlikely (sensitivity about 97% in the Cochrane review). A high venous PCO₂ is less useful: specificity is only about 54%.

errors.out_of_range_paco2: PaCO₂ must be between 5 and 150 mmHg.
errors.out_of_range_hco3: HCO₃⁻ must be between 2 and 60 mmol/L.
errors.out_of_range_na: Na⁺ must be between 100 and 180 mmol/L.
errors.out_of_range_cl: Cl⁻ must be between 60 and 140 mmol/L.
errors.out_of_range_albumin: Albumin must be between 0.5 and 6 g/dL.

hagma.title: High anion gap metabolic acidosis — GOLD MARK
hagma.note: Check lactate, ketones, creatinine, a salicylate level, and the osmolar gap when toxic alcohols are possible.

nagma.title: Normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis
items: GI bicarbonate loss: severe diarrhea, small-bowel or pancreatic fistula, biliary drainage

metabolic_alkalosis.title: Metabolic alkalosis
items: Chloride depletion: vomiting or NG suction, diuretics, post-hypercapnia, chloride-losing villous adenoma
Potassium depletion / mineralocorticoid excess: primary or secondary hyperaldosteronism, Cushing's, licorice, Bartter's, severe hypokalemia
Added base: bicarbonate, milk-alkali syndrome, citrate from massive transfusion, recovery from organic acidosis
metabolic_alkalosis.note: Urine chloride helps once diuretics have worn off: low in chloride depletion, high (> 20 mmol/L) in mineralocorticoid excess, severe potassium depletion, or active diuretic effect.

respiratory_acidosis.title: Respiratory acidosis
items: Central depression: opioids, sedatives, anesthetics, CNS injury, obesity hypoventilation, high cord lesion (C4 or above)
Nerve or muscle: Guillain-Barré, myasthenia, neuromuscular blockers, organophosphates
Lung or chest wall: COPD exacerbation, severe asthma, flail chest, pneumothorax, ARDS, pulmonary edema
CO₂ production with fixed ventilation (malignant hyperthermia) or rebreathing / laparoscopic CO₂

respiratory_alkalosis.title: Respiratory alkalosis
items: Central: pain, anxiety, head injury, stroke, salicylates, pregnancy (progesterone), sepsis, liver disease
Pulmonary: pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, asthma, pulmonary edema

toolContent.clinicalTakeaway: Name the cause, not just the disorder: 'metabolic acidosis' is only useful once it becomes DKA, lactic acidosis or a toxic alcohol. A gas is a snapshot — recheck after treatment.
toolContent.whyThisMatters: Most missed acid-base diagnoses are the second disorder: a respiratory acidosis in a tiring patient with DKA, a metabolic alkalosis hiding a gap acidosis, a salicylate patient whose pH looks reassuring. Checking compensation and the delta ratio on every gas catches them.

buildNote: Code-backed tool (engine: builtin, tool: acid-base). Math in web/src/lib/acidBaseEngine.js and ios/Sources/Calc/AcidBaseEngine.swift; both run tools/fixtures/acid-base-golden-vectors.json. Design choices beyond the sources: the ± 2 band Brandis gives for chronic respiratory alkalosis is applied to all four respiratory rules; a Henderson-Hasselbalch mismatch above 0.05 pH units is flagged; when pH is out of range but PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ are both within their reference ranges, the component with the larger deviation (scaled to each half-range) is called primary; at normal pH with both values shifted the same way, the chronic respiratory rule is tested before calling the disorder mixed. Venous mode: 'normal' venous PCO2 for the rule-out flag is taken as ≤ 45 mmHg (conservative); the anion gap and delta ratio use the measured venous HCO3 because gap normals come from serum (venous) chemistry.
